The class $\mathcal{G}$ requires that all nonlinear irreducible characters have degrees with the **same** number of distinct prime divisors, say $k$.

If $G\in\mathcal{G}$ is non-solvable, then $G/R(G)$ is a direct product of non-abelian simple groups. If there were two or more factors, taking nonlinear characters from different factors would produce tensor-product degrees whose number of distinct prime divisors exceeds $k$; hence $G/R(G)\cong S$ is a single non-abelian simple group. Inflating characters from $S$ shows that $S$ itself must lie in $\mathcal{G}$ with the same $k$.

Every finite simple group of Lie type has a Steinberg character of degree a power of the defining characteristic, forcing $k=1$. Alternating and sporadic groups likewise admit nonlinear characters of prime degree, so again $k=1$. Thus every nonlinear degree of $S$ must be a **prime power**.

Checking the simple groups:
- $A_5\cong\operatorname{PSL}(2,4)\cong\operatorname{PSL}(2,5)$ has nonlinear degrees $3,3,4,5$ — all prime powers. Hence $A_5\in\mathcal{G}$, contributing primes $\{2,3,5\}$.
- $\operatorname{PSL}(2,8)$ has nonlinear degrees $7$ (four times), $8$, $9$ (three times) — i.e. $7,2^3,3^2$, all prime powers. Hence $\operatorname{PSL}(2,8)\in\mathcal{G}$, contributing primes $\{2,3,7\}$.
- All other $\operatorname{PSL}(2,q)$ fail (e.g. $\operatorname{PSL}(2,7)$ has degree $6$, $\operatorname{PSL}(2,16)$ has degree $15$, etc.). All remaining simple groups (alternating $n\geq6$, sporadic, higher-rank Lie type) possess nonlinear degrees that are not prime powers.

Schur covers and other proper extensions of these simples introduce characters whose degrees are not prime powers (e.g. $\operatorname{SL}(2,5)$ has degree $6$), so they are excluded. Direct products with abelian groups preserve the degree set and introduce no new primes.

Therefore
$$P=\{2,3,5,7\},$$
and the sum of all elements of $P$ is
